questions.title: Can a court dismiss a copyright claim based on fair use at the Rule 12(b)(6) pleading stage?
questions.question_body: I am confused about the procedural timing here. Usually, fair use is treated as an affirmative defense, which I thought meant it was a factual determination made after discovery. In Santos v. Kimmel, the court affirmed a dismissal under Rule 12(b)(6), stating fair use was "so clearly established by a complaint." How is it possible to determine fair use without a full evidentiary record?

questions.title: How does the 'reasonable observer' test resolve conflicts between a creator's intent and a user's purpose in transformative use?
questions.question_body: In this case, Santos argued that the use wasn't transformative because Kimmel actually paid for and 'instigated' the videos, meaning the purpose of the creation was aligned with Kimmel's eventual use. However, the court held that transformativeness depends on what a 'reasonable observer' thinks, not the subjective intent of the parties. If the defendant essentially commissioned the work to be mocked, why does the 'reasonable observer' standard override the actual intent of the creation?

questions.title: Does 'bad faith' or fraudulent acquisition of a work negate a fair use defense?
questions.question_body: I'm struggling with the court's treatment of the Harper & Row precedent. Santos argued that because Kimmel used fictitious names to trick him into making the videos, this 'bad faith' should nullify the fair use defense. The court mentioned that the Supreme Court has 'distanced itself' from the requirement of good faith. Does this mean a person can essentially commit fraud to obtain a copyrighted work and still successfully plead fair use if the final output is transformative?

questions.title: Under what circumstances does the Copyright Act 'preempt' state law breach of contract claims?
questions.question_body: The court mentions that the District Court dismissed Santos's contract claims because they were 'preempted by the Copyright Act.' I don't understand how a contract claim (which is about an agreement between parties) can be preempted by copyright law (which is about the right to control a work). What does it mean for a contract claim to be 'qualitatively' similar to a copyright claim in a way that triggers preemption?

questions.title: When is a non-signatory considered a third-party beneficiary of a platform's Terms of Service?
questions.question_body: Santos tried to sue for a breach of the Cameo Terms of Service (TOS), which Kimmel agreed to. The court dismissed this because Santos wasn't a party to the contract and there was no 'express declaration' of third-party beneficiary status. If a platform's TOS is specifically designed to regulate the behavior of users to protect the sellers on that platform, why isn't that an implicit third-party beneficiary right?

questions.title: Is an actual 'out-of-pocket' monetary loss required for a fraudulent inducement claim to survive a motion to dismiss?
questions.question_body: The court affirmed the dismissal of the fraudulent inducement claim because Santos failed to allege any 'out-of-pocket loss.' I thought that fraudulent inducement was about the deception and the fact that the plaintiff relied on that deception to their detriment. If someone is tricked into providing a service, is that not 'detriment,' or does New York law specifically require a quantifiable cash loss for the claim to be valid?
